screens.title: What is a Snowflake Account?
screens.narratorSegment: A Snowflake account is the atomic administrative unit that holds your warehouses, databases, and users. It is provisioned in a single cloud provider and a single geographic region, which means all compute and storage for that account are tied to that location by default. Practically, that isolation provides security boundaries: one account cannot accidentally access another customer's data. It also gives independent resource management: credits, warehouses, and parameter defaults are tracked per account. For example, if your company creates separate accounts for development and production, you can tune account-level parameters differently and avoid interference. A common misconception is that an account can span multiple clouds or regions; this is not true. If you need multi-region presence or multi-cloud coverage, use multiple accounts and consider Organizations and replication features. Key takeaway: treat the account as your secure, regionally located workspace and design environments and governance around it. Reflect: for your teams, what workloads belong in a shared account and what should live in a separate account? What is a Snowflake Account? means provision accounts per environment or compliance boundary so each account has clear ownership and defaults.. In practical terms, an isolated workspace provisioned on one cloud provider and region. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is a Snowflake Account?
Definition
An isolated environment for data warehousing
  • Provisioned on a single cloud provider and region.
  • Contains warehouses, databases, users, and parameters.
  • Provides a security and billing boundary.
Concrete example
A company uses one account for production in an EU region for customer data, and a separate account in another region for development to isolate testing workloads and billing.
Key Takeaway

Design accounts around ownership, compliance, and operational boundaries. Do not assume an account spans regions.

Why isolation matters
  • Security: limits blast radius of misconfiguration or breach.
  • Performance: resource limits and warehouses are scoped per account.
  • Compliance: regional provisioning aligns to data residency rules.
Common mistake
Choosing a single account to try to cover all regions or environments. Instead, use multiple accounts and manage them via an Organization when centralization is needed.
Reflect
Which workloads in your organization need strict regional isolation? Use that as the primary driver for separate accounts.

screens.title: Reading the Snowflake Account URL
screens.narratorSegment: The account URL is a small but critical piece of operational knowledge. Typical URLs look like: https://account_identifier. region_id. snowflakecomputing. com. The account identifier is a unique string that refers to your specific Snowflake account. The region ID encodes both the cloud provider and the geographic region, for example aws_us_east_1 or azure_west_europe. Knowing these parts matters for two main reasons: connectivity and compliance. First, many clients and tools need the exact account identifier and region to establish a connection. If you use the wrong region, clients may fail to connect or connect to an unexpected account. Second, the region ID determines where data is physically stored and processed, which is essential for regulatory compliance such as GDPR. A common misconception is that the account identifier implies location; it does not. Always read the region_id in the URL to confirm residency. Practice example: when you see a URL with aws_eu_central_1, you can conclude the account is hosted in AWS Frankfurt and must follow EU data residency requirements. Question: does your URL match your expected compliance region? Reading the Snowflake Account URL means account identifier = which account. region id = which cloud and geography; this determines residency and connectivity endpoints.. In practical terms, identify the account identifier and region id and why they matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Reading the Account URL
Structure
https://<account_identifier>.<region_id>.snowflakecomputing.com
The account_identifier is unique to your account. The region_id indicates the cloud and geographic site.
Concrete example
If the URL contains aws_eu_central_1, that means the account is hosted on AWS in the EU Central region. This signals EU data residency and lower latency for EU users.
Key Takeaway

Always confirm the region_id for compliance and correct client connections; the account identifier alone does not specify location.

Why this matters
  • Connectivity: clients require the correct endpoint to connect to the intended account.
  • Compliance: region determines where data is stored and processed.
  • Latency: pick regions near your users and data sources.
Common mistake
Assuming the account identifier shows location. Instead, rely on region_id when validating compliance or planning replication.
Reflect
When you inspect your account URL today, does the region align with regulatory and proximity requirements for your primary users?

screens.title: Regions, Data Residency, and Latency
screens.narratorSegment: Region selection is both technical and legal. The region_id you choose for an account determines where data is physically stored and processed. For compliance, this can be decisive: regulations may require that customer data stays within a geographic boundary. From a performance perspective, choosing a region near your users and primary data sources reduces network latency and improves query responsiveness. When planning, map three things: the regulatory restrictions for your data, the geographic distribution of your users, and the location of your upstream data sources. A common error is to choose the closest cloud region without checking residency rules. For enterprise scenarios you may need multi-region deployments; Snowflake supports cross-region replication, but that requires additional accounts and configuration. Example: for EU customer data, provision an account in an EU region and consider replication to a secondary EU region for disaster recovery. Key takeaway: region choice is a policy decision as much as a latency choice. Who decides region selection in your organization, and what constraints should guide that decision? Regions, Data Residency, and Latency means pick region to satisfy both compliance and latency; replication across regions requires additional accounts and planning.. In practical terms, choose regions based on compliance, user location, and data sources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Regions & Residency
Comparison: Latency vs Compliance
Latency-focused
Choose a region closest to users and data sources for best performance.
Compliance-focused
Choose a region that satisfies legal requirements even if slightly farther from users.
Concrete example
If most users and sources are in Europe and regulations mandate EU storage, provision the account in an EU region such as azure_west_europe or aws_eu_central_1 to meet residency and latency needs.
Key Takeaway

Treat region selection as a governance decision. Document constraints and plan replication for DR rather than relying on a single account to satisfy all needs.

Planning checklist
  • Regulatory requirements for each dataset.
  • Primary user locations and acceptable latency.
  • Where upstream data sources live.
  • Disaster recovery and replication strategy.
Common mistake
Choosing region purely on cost or convenience without validating residency. That can create compliance risk even if performance is good.
Reflect
Which data sets in your organization have strict residency rules and need dedicated accounts in a compliant region?

screens.title: What is a Snowflake Organization?
screens.narratorSegment: A Snowflake Organization gives you a control plane above individual accounts. It is designed for larger deployments where a business needs multiple accounts for isolation, different environments, or geographic separation. Within an Organization you can consolidate billing across accounts, simplify certain administrative workflows, and enable cross-account replication patterns later on. Think of an Organization as a folder of accounts: each account still operates independently, but the Organization provides centralized visibility and governance. For example, a company might create an Organization that contains a production account in Europe, a production account in the US, and separate development accounts for each region. That structure makes it easier to track costs and coordinate replication or backup strategies across accounts. A misconception is expecting Organizations to blur isolation; they do not remove account boundaries for data unless you configure replication or sharing. Key takeaway: use Organizations when you need centralized billing and cross-account operational control while preserving account-level isolation. What is a Snowflake Organization? means use organizations to centralize billing and cross-account management while keeping accounts isolated for security and compliance.. In practical terms, a top-level entity to manage multiple accounts centrally. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Snowflake Organization
Definition
Top-level container for multiple accounts
Provides centralized billing, visibility, and coordination for cross-account features like replication. Accounts remain independent workspaces.
Concrete scenario
An enterprise creates an Organization with production accounts in two regions, plus development and staging accounts, so billing and governance can be centralized while teams work in separate accounts.
Key Takeaway

Organizations simplify management across many accounts but do not remove account-level isolation unless you explicitly configure sharing or replication.

Benefits
  • Consolidated billing across linked accounts.
  • Centralized control plane for administrative visibility.
  • Simplifies multi-account replication and governance.
Common mistake
Expecting an Organization to automatically unify data or permissions across accounts. You still configure sharing, replication, and roles per account as needed.
Reflect
If your company has multiple lines of business or strict environment separation, consider an Organization to centralize billing and coordination while keeping accounts separate.

screens.title: When to Use Organizations
screens.narratorSegment: Organizations are valuable when your deployment grows beyond a single account. Typical use cases include separating environments like development, staging, and production into distinct accounts, isolating sensitive datasets by business unit or geography, and managing consolidated billing across all accounts. Another benefit is simplifying cross-account replication and disaster recovery: an Organization gives you a central place to coordinate those efforts. It is especially useful for large enterprises where teams require autonomy but finance and security need oversight. That said, Organizations add a level of governance and should be used when the advantages outweigh the extra operational coordination. A misconception is that Organizations remove the need for per-account governance; they actually complement it by offering higher-level controls. Example: a multinational company might use an Organization to hold separate accounts for each region to comply with data residency rules while keeping finance and policy consistent across accounts. Key question: does your environment need centralized billing and coordinated replication, or will a single account suffice? When to Use Organizations means adopt organizations for multi-account governance, consolidated billing, and coordinated replication—particularly in enterprises with strict separation needs.. screens.title: Account, User, and Session Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Snowflake parameters follow a clear hierarchy: account-level defaults apply to everyone, user-level parameters apply to a specific user and override account defaults, and session-level parameters apply only to the current session and override both user and account levels. This structure gives you flexibility: set conservative defaults at the account level to protect the environment, provide broader allowances to specific users when necessary, and use session overrides for temporary, one-off needs. A practical example is STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS. You may set a 3600-second default at the account level to prevent very long queries, then give an ETL user a 14400-second user-level value for scheduled jobs, and for an ad-hoc analysis session a session-level 600-second override to limit accidental long runs. A common misconception is that changing a session parameter modifies account defaults; it does not — session changes are ephemeral. Key takeaway: use account parameters for safe defaults, user parameters for role-specific needs, and session parameters for temporary adjustments. How would you set defaults to balance safety and power in your organization? Account, User, and Session Parameters means account (default) < user (override) < session (temporary override). use this to balance safety and operational flexibility.. In practical terms, understand the hierarchy and how overrides work. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Account (default) < User (override) < Session (temporary override). Use this to balance safety and operational flexibility.

content.html:

Hierarchy
  1. Account: defaults for everyone unless overridden.
  2. User: specific to a user; overrides account.
  3. Session: temporary for the current session; overrides user and account.
Concrete example
STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS set at account, raised for ETL user at user-level, and temporarily shortened for a troubleshooting session at session-level.
Key Takeaway

Set safe account defaults, allow user overrides when needed, and use session overrides for short-lived needs without changing defaults.

Operational tips

  • Use session-level changes for debugging or temporary workloads.
  • Monitor for unexpected session overrides in audit logs.
Common mistake
Assuming a session SET persists. Session changes revert when the session ends and do not change account or user defaults.
Reflect
Which parameters should never be lowered or removed at the account level for safety in your environment?

keyIdea.text: SHOW PARAMETERS IN ACCOUNT; SHOW PARAMETERS IN SESSION; ALTER ACCOUNT SET ...; ALTER SESSION SET ... — use correct scope for the change you intend.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Inspecting & Setting Parameters
Reference commands
-- View account parameters (requires monitoring/account privileges)
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
SHOW PARAMETERS IN ACCOUNT;

-- View current session parameters
SHOW PARAMETERS IN SESSION;

-- Set a temporary session parameter (30 minutes)
ALTER SESSION SET STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS = 1800;

-- Reset session parameter to default
ALTER SESSION SET STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS = DEFAULT;
Key Takeaway

Use SHOW to inspect effective values and ALTER with the correct scope to change behavior. Session changes are temporary.

Walkthrough scenario
1) As ACCOUNTADMIN, run SHOW PARAMETERS IN ACCOUNT and note STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS. 2) Run SHOW PARAMETERS IN SESSION and compare the value. 3) ALTER SESSION SET STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS = 1800 and re-run SHOW PARAMETERS IN SESSION to verify the session now shows 1800.
Common mistake
Running ALTER ACCOUNT SET when you intended a temporary session change. Always confirm scope before running ALTER commands.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Session Example
Step-by-step
-- Check account default
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
SHOW PARAMETERS IN ACCOUNT;

-- Check current session value
SHOW PARAMETERS IN SESSION;

An analyst running a complex transform increases session timeout to allow long-running steps, then resets it after completion so other sessions retain safe defaults.
Common mistake
Forgetting to reset a session or relying on session changes for persistent needs. Use ALTER ACCOUNT SET for permanent change when appropriate.

screens.title: Roles, Privileges, and ACCOUNTADMIN
screens.narratorSegment: Administrative roles control who can change account settings and perform sensitive tasks. The ACCOUNTADMIN role is the most powerful in a Snowflake account: it can create users and roles, manage warehouses and databases, and alter account parameters. Because of its power, best practice is to reserve ACCOUNTADMIN usage and build narrower administrative roles for daily operations. For example, use a SYSADMIN role to manage warehouses and databases, and a USERADMIN role for user and role lifecycle tasks. This separation follows the principle of least privilege: give people only the access they need to perform their tasks. A common mistake is using ACCOUNTADMIN for convenience; that increases risk of accidental change. Concrete example: create a role that only has privileges to create and manage warehouses, and assign that role to the operations team, leaving ACCOUNTADMIN for emergency or cross-cutting tasks. Key takeaway: design administrative roles intentionally and audit assignments regularly to reduce security and operational risk. Roles, Privileges, and ACCOUNTADMIN means minimize use of accountadmin. create focused administrative roles and apply least privilege for routine tasks.. In practical terms, principle of least privilege for secure account administration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Manage warehouses and databases.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Governance Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Organizations and accounts fail in practice when structural decisions are driven by convenience rather than governance. Common mistakes include choosing a region solely for convenience without checking data residency laws, using ACCOUNTADMIN for daily tasks, and relying on session changes when permanent defaults are required. To govern safely, document account purposes (production, dev), required residency constraints, and parameter policies that define which settings can be changed and at what scope. Implement role-based boundaries: who can alter account parameters, who can run ALTER ACCOUNT, and who can perform billing tasks in the Organization. Another pattern is to centralize sensitive policy decisions in a small governance team and delegate operational tasks to finer-grained admin roles. Example: maintain an approved-regions list and require justification before provisioning a new account in a non-standard region. Key takeaway: combine policy, role design, and documented parameter defaults to reduce mistakes and keep your Snowflake estate manageable. Common Mistakes and Governance Patterns means prevent mistakes with documented policies: approved regions, parameter change rules, and least-privilege role assignments.. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a clear mental model of Snowflake accounts and Organizations and why those boundaries matter. A Snowflake account is an isolated, secure workspace provisioned on a single cloud provider and region. That location shows up in your account URL and determines where data lives, which affects compliance, latency, and disaster recovery. Organizations sit above accounts to let you manage many accounts together—useful for enterprises that separate development, staging, and production or run accounts across business units. You'll also learn how account parameters control defaults such as the statement timeout, how those parameters can be overridden at user or session scope, and why administrative roles like ACCOUNTADMIN should be scoped carefully. As we go, notice practical examples you can use today: inspecting parameters, setting a session timeout, and choosing a compliant region for your workloads. By the end, you should be able to explain the account URL structure, set a session parameter for single-session needs, and describe when an Organization is the right choice. Think about your own environment: where would you place production data and who should hold ACCOUNTADMIN privileges?

These learning objectives define practical skills you will practice during this chapter. You will be able to differentiate a Snowflake account from a Snowflake Organization, explaining how an account is an isolated workspace provisioned on a single cloud provider and region, while an Organization groups multiple accounts for centralized management. You will also identify and read the components of a Snowflake account URL so you can confirm data residency and connect clients correctly. Managing parameters is a hands-on skill: you'll learn how account parameters act as defaults while user and session parameters override them, and you'll practice setting a session-level parameter for temporary behavior changes. Finally, you'll understand how region selection affects latency and compliance, and why administrative roles like ACCOUNTADMIN should be scoped to follow least privilege. Each objective pairs a practical command or inspection task with an explanation of why it matters, preparing you to manage accounts and explain trade-offs to stakeholders.

This second objectives slide focuses on concrete operational skills and their reasons. You will practice inspecting account parameters with SHOW PARAMETERS IN ACCOUNT, and comparing them to session parameters with SHOW PARAMETERS IN SESSION to see inheritance in action. You'll learn to set a temporary session-level parameter using ALTER SESSION SET so you can tune a single user session without changing defaults for everyone. Another objective is to reason about roles: identify which tasks require ACCOUNTADMIN and which are safer under more restricted admin roles, and practice assigning responsibilities using the principle of least privilege. Finally, you'll consider region selection by mapping your data residency and latency needs to provider regions—this helps you avoid common mistakes like locating EU customer data outside the EU. Each objective links a CLI or UI action to a compliance, performance, or governance outcome so you're ready to apply these skills immediately.

A Snowflake account is the atomic administrative unit that holds your warehouses, databases, and users. It is provisioned in a single cloud provider and a single geographic region, which means all compute and storage for that account are tied to that location by default. Practically, that isolation provides security boundaries: one account cannot accidentally access another customer's data. It also gives independent resource management: credits, warehouses, and parameter defaults are tracked per account. For example, if your company creates separate accounts for development and production, you can tune account-level parameters differently and avoid interference. A common misconception is that an account can span multiple clouds or regions; this is not true. If you need multi-region presence or multi-cloud coverage, use multiple accounts and consider Organizations and replication features. Key takeaway: treat the account as your secure, regionally located workspace and design environments and governance around it. Reflect: for your teams, what workloads belong in a shared account and what should live in a separate account? What is a Snowflake Account? means provision accounts per environment or compliance boundary so each account has clear ownership and defaults.. In practical terms, an isolated workspace provisioned on one cloud provider and region. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The account URL is a small but critical piece of operational knowledge. Typical URLs look like: https://account_identifier. region_id. snowflakecomputing. com. The account identifier is a unique string that refers to your specific Snowflake account. The region ID encodes both the cloud provider and the geographic region, for example aws_us_east_1 or azure_west_europe. Knowing these parts matters for two main reasons: connectivity and compliance. First, many clients and tools need the exact account identifier and region to establish a connection. If you use the wrong region, clients may fail to connect or connect to an unexpected account. Second, the region ID determines where data is physically stored and processed, which is essential for regulatory compliance such as GDPR. A common misconception is that the account identifier implies location; it does not. Always read the region_id in the URL to confirm residency. Practice example: when you see a URL with aws_eu_central_1, you can conclude the account is hosted in AWS Frankfurt and must follow EU data residency requirements. Question: does your URL match your expected compliance region? Reading the Snowflake Account URL means account identifier = which account. region id = which cloud and geography; this determines residency and connectivity endpoints.. In practical terms, identify the account identifier and region id and why they matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Region selection is both technical and legal. The region_id you choose for an account determines where data is physically stored and processed. For compliance, this can be decisive: regulations may require that customer data stays within a geographic boundary. From a performance perspective, choosing a region near your users and primary data sources reduces network latency and improves query responsiveness. When planning, map three things: the regulatory restrictions for your data, the geographic distribution of your users, and the location of your upstream data sources. A common error is to choose the closest cloud region without checking residency rules. For enterprise scenarios you may need multi-region deployments; Snowflake supports cross-region replication, but that requires additional accounts and configuration. Example: for EU customer data, provision an account in an EU region and consider replication to a secondary EU region for disaster recovery. Key takeaway: region choice is a policy decision as much as a latency choice. Who decides region selection in your organization, and what constraints should guide that decision? Regions, Data Residency, and Latency means pick region to satisfy both compliance and latency; replication across regions requires additional accounts and planning.. In practical terms, choose regions based on compliance, user location, and data sources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Snowflake Organization gives you a control plane above individual accounts. It is designed for larger deployments where a business needs multiple accounts for isolation, different environments, or geographic separation. Within an Organization you can consolidate billing across accounts, simplify certain administrative workflows, and enable cross-account replication patterns later on. Think of an Organization as a folder of accounts: each account still operates independently, but the Organization provides centralized visibility and governance. For example, a company might create an Organization that contains a production account in Europe, a production account in the US, and separate development accounts for each region. That structure makes it easier to track costs and coordinate replication or backup strategies across accounts. A misconception is expecting Organizations to blur isolation; they do not remove account boundaries for data unless you configure replication or sharing. Key takeaway: use Organizations when you need centralized billing and cross-account operational control while preserving account-level isolation. What is a Snowflake Organization? means use organizations to centralize billing and cross-account management while keeping accounts isolated for security and compliance.. In practical terms, a top-level entity to manage multiple accounts centrally. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Organizations are valuable when your deployment grows beyond a single account. Typical use cases include separating environments like development, staging, and production into distinct accounts, isolating sensitive datasets by business unit or geography, and managing consolidated billing across all accounts. Another benefit is simplifying cross-account replication and disaster recovery: an Organization gives you a central place to coordinate those efforts. Snowflake parameters follow a clear hierarchy: account-level defaults apply to everyone, user-level parameters apply to a specific user and override account defaults, and session-level parameters apply only to the current session and override both user and account levels. This structure gives you flexibility: set conservative defaults at the account level to protect the environment, provide broader allowances to specific users when necessary, and use session overrides for temporary, one-off needs. A practical example is STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS. You may set a 3600-second default at the account level to prevent very long queries, then give an ETL user a 14400-second user-level value for scheduled jobs, and for an ad-hoc analysis session a session-level 600-second override to limit accidental long runs. A common misconception is that changing a session parameter modifies account defaults; it does not — session changes are ephemeral. Key takeaway: use account parameters for safe defaults, user parameters for role-specific needs, and session parameters for temporary adjustments. This screen walks through the key commands you'll use to inspect and set parameters. SHOW PARAMETERS IN ACCOUNT lists account-level settings and is typically run by a role with monitoring or account privileges. SHOW PARAMETERS IN SESSION shows the current session's effective values and reveals what is inherited or overridden. To change an account parameter you use ALTER ACCOUNT SET parameter = value, which requires appropriate administrative roles. To set a session parameter temporarily use ALTER SESSION SET parameter = value; this change affects only the current session. Practice example: run SHOW PARAMETERS IN ACCOUNT to find STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS, then run SHOW PARAMETERS IN SESSION to compare. Next, run ALTER SESSION SET STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS = 1800 to allow a 30-minute timeout for your session and then re-run SHOW PARAMETERS IN SESSION to confirm. Administrative roles control who can change account settings and perform sensitive tasks. The ACCOUNTADMIN role is the most powerful in a Snowflake account: it can create users and roles, manage warehouses and databases, and alter account parameters. Because of its power, best practice is to reserve ACCOUNTADMIN usage and build narrower administrative roles for daily operations. For example, use a SYSADMIN role to manage warehouses and databases, and a USERADMIN role for user and role lifecycle tasks. This separation follows the principle of least privilege: give people only the access they need to perform their tasks. A common mistake is using ACCOUNTADMIN for convenience; that increases risk of accidental change. Concrete example: create a role that only has privileges to create and manage warehouses, and assign that role to the operations team, leaving ACCOUNTADMIN for emergency or cross-cutting tasks. Key takeaway: design administrative roles intentionally and audit assignments regularly to reduce security and operational risk. Organizations and accounts fail in practice when structural decisions are driven by convenience rather than governance. Common mistakes include choosing a region solely for convenience without checking data residency laws, using ACCOUNTADMIN for daily tasks, and relying on session changes when permanent defaults are required. To govern safely, document account purposes (production, dev), required residency constraints, and parameter policies that define which settings can be changed and at what scope. Let's summarize the essential concepts to remember. First, a Snowflake account is an isolated workspace provisioned on a single cloud provider and region; the account identifier and region ID in the URL tell you where data is located. Second, Snowflake Organizations provide a top-level control plane to manage multiple accounts, consolidate billing, and coordinate cross-account replication while preserving account isolation. Third, parameters follow a hierarchy: account defaults can be overridden by user-level settings, which can be temporarily overridden by session-level settings. Each of these concepts has operational consequences: pick regions to meet compliance, use Organizations for enterprise management when needed, and set parameters at the proper scope to avoid accidental global changes.
